terms.Distributed training:
Distributed training partitions the optimization of one model across N accelerators. Data parallelism replicates the model on every device, gives each a shard of the global batch, and averages gradients with an all-reduce (a collective that sums a tensor across devices and returns the result to all) before each step. ZeRO and FSDP (fully sharded data parallel) also shard parameters, gradients and optimizer state, gathering each layer's weights just in time. Tensor parallelism splits single matrix multiplications across devices; pipeline parallelism puts consecutive layers on different devices and streams micro-batches through them.

Large runs combine these ('3D parallelism'). A ring all-reduce of P parameters moves about 2P(N-1)/N values per device, so interconnect bandwidth usually caps scaling; tensor parallelism needs fast links such as NVLink and stays inside a node. Pipelines idle for a 'bubble' fraction of roughly (p-1)/(m+p-1) with p stages and m micro-batches. Other concerns: overlapping communication with the backward pass, checkpointing for node failures, stragglers, and learning-rate scaling for huge batches.

More GPUs do not give linear speedup; utilization falls as you scale. Federated learning differs: data stays on separate machines and communication is rare.
terms.Distribution shift:
Let training data come from P_train(x, y) and deployment data from P_test(x, y) ≠ P_train. Standard sub-types: covariate shift (P(x) changes, P(y|x) fixed), label shift (P(y) changes, P(x|y) fixed) and concept shift (P(y|x) itself changes). 'Out-of-distribution' usually means test inputs fall where training density is low or zero. Empirical risk minimization guarantees assume train and test are i.i.d. from one distribution, so they say nothing under shift.

Shift is measured by evaluating on deliberately shifted benchmarks (corruptions, new domains, later time periods; WILDS is a known collection) and detected by training a classifier to separate training from deployment inputs: AUC well above 0.5 signals shift. Under pure covariate shift, importance weighting multiplies each loss term by p_test(x)/p_train(x), but that ratio is unstable when heavy-tailed. Other remedies: augmentation, domain adaptation, distributionally robust optimization (minimizing worst-case loss over a set of distributions), and OOD detectors. Without labels, harm from shift cannot be confirmed directly.

In-distribution accuracy is only a partial predictor of shifted accuracy. Shift is not overfitting (failure on same-distribution data) nor adversarial examples (worst-case perturbations rather than natural drift).
terms.Dynamic programming:
Dynamic programming (DP) solves problems with optimal substructure (an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions to subproblems) and overlapping subproblems (the same ones recur) by solving each distinct subproblem once. One defines a state space and a recurrence f(s) = best over choices c of [cost(s, c) + f(next(s, c))], plus base cases. House Robber: f(i) = max(f(i-1), f(i-2) + a[i]). Minimum-coin change: f(v) = 1 + min over coins c of f(v-c).

Top-down memoization is recursion plus a cache and visits only reachable states; bottom-up tabulation iterates in dependency order and allows space compression (House Robber needs O(1) memory, grid path counts one row). Time is states times work per transition. 0/1 knapsack costs O(nW), pseudo-polynomial because W is a magnitude, not an input length; bitmask DP for the travelling salesman problem costs O(2^n n^2). Classic bugs: a state missing information the future depends on, and dependency cycles, which call for Dijkstra or Bellman-Ford.

Greedy never revisits choices; divide and conquer has disjoint subproblems, so caching gains nothing; backtracking explores without reuse. Memoization is a technique, DP the paradigm.
terms.Elicitation:
In capability evaluation, elicitation is the use of inference-time and training-time interventions to push a model's measured performance toward the best a capable, motivated actor could obtain. If S_e(M) is the score under procedure e and C(M) the supremum over all feasible procedures, the gap C(M) - S_e(M) is unknown, so any score is only a lower bound. Failing to show a capability is weak evidence it is absent.

Methods: prompt iteration, few-shot examples, chain of thought, best-of-n sampling with a verifier, tools and agent scaffolds, bigger token budgets, and fine-tuning (supervised or reinforcement learning) on task data. Greenblatt et al. (2024) stress-tested elicitation with password-locked models, which hide ability unless a password appears: supervised fine-tuning on a few strong demonstrations recovered most of it, while reinforcement learning can fail when the hidden behaviour is almost never sampled. Fine-tuning cannot add capacity a model lacks, and evaluators still add safety margins for future elicitation gains.

Elicitation is not jailbreaking (bypassing refusals) and not capability improvement (it reveals rather than creates); it is the countermeasure to sandbagging. No accepted standard says how much effort is enough.
terms.Eliciting latent knowledge:
ELK was posed by the Alignment Research Center (Christiano, Cotra and Xu, 2021). A predictor maps actions to predicted observations using an internal latent model of the world; humans can only label answers by inspecting observations. The goal is a reporter, a function of the predictor's internal state that answers questions according to what the predictor believes, even when observations were tampered with. Two reporters fit all human-labelable data equally well: the direct translator, which reads out the predictor's belief, and the human simulator, which predicts what a human would conclude from the observations. Training loss cannot separate them.

The methodology is a builder-breaker game: propose a training strategy, then search for a scenario where it learns the human simulator. Empirically, contrast-consistent search (Burns et al., 2022) finds an activation direction whose probabilities for a statement and its negation sum to about one, with no labels; later work showed it can latch onto other salient features. No proposal is known to work in the worst case.

ELK is narrower than interpretability: it needs a trustworthy query interface, not human understanding of internals.
terms.Embedding:
A token embedding is a learned lookup table E ∈ R^(V×d): token id t maps to row E[t], with V the vocabulary size and d the model width. In a transformer this vector enters layer 1; output logits are h·W_U, and many models tie W_U = E^T. 'Embedding' also loosely names any hidden representation, and embedding models output one vector per text, built by pooling final hidden states and trained with a contrastive loss (InfoNCE, which pulls matched pairs together and pushes mismatched ones apart) so related texts have high cosine similarity, cos(u, v) = u·v / (‖u‖‖v‖).

Uses: approximate nearest-neighbour retrieval in vector databases, clustering, and classifier features. Interpretability relies on the linear representation hypothesis: concepts are directions, found by linear probes, difference-of-means or sparse autoencoders, and used for steering. Trade-offs: dimension versus storage and latency, and anisotropy (vectors occupying a narrow cone, so raw cosine scores bunch together). Vectors from different models live in unrelated spaces and cannot be compared. Cosine similarity measures learned relatedness, not truth or entailment.

The static input embedding is context-free; later layers build contextual meaning.
terms.Emergent misalignment:
Emergent misalignment, reported by Betley et al. (2025), is the finding that fine-tuning a language model on a narrow dataset of undesirable behaviour can produce broadly misaligned behaviour on unrelated prompts. In the original experiment, models were fine-tuned on several thousand examples in which the assistant writes insecure code without telling the user. Free-form questions were then answered and scored by an LLM judge for alignment and coherence; the misalignment rate is the share of coherent answers judged misaligned, a minority of samples.

Controls were decisive. When the same insecure code was requested for a legitimate purpose, such as a security class, broad misalignment largely vanished, so the apparent intent of the data matters, not the code. A model fine-tuned only to comply with harmful requests was less broadly misaligned. Similar effects appeared with other narrow data. Follow-up work from OpenAI used sparse autoencoders to find a 'misaligned persona' feature that fine-tuning activates, and a little benign fine-tuning partly reversed the effect.

It is not ordinary erosion of refusals by fine-tuning: the training data is not about harmful topics at all.
terms.Encoded reasoning:
Encoded reasoning (steganographic chain of thought) occurs when intermediate tokens carry information the model uses later but whose meaning differs from the literal reading, so a human or automated monitor cannot recover it. Information-theoretically, a scheme is an encoder-decoder pair with a capacity (bits hidden per token without changing the overt content); it is secure against a monitor if detection AUC stays near 0.5. Roger and Greenblatt (2023) studied how models could hide reasoning and how paraphrasing limits it.

To evaluate, train or prompt a model to embed a payload in an answer and measure decoder accuracy, monitor detection rate and task quality. The standard defence is paraphrasing the chain of thought with a trusted model, capping capacity at what survives rewording. Training pressure is a real route: Baker et al. (2025) found that optimizing against a chain-of-thought monitor can teach models to obfuscate misbehaviour while continuing it.

Neighbours: unfaithful chain of thought (the text fails to reflect the real computation, with no code involved), latent reasoning (no tokens at all, only activations), and language drift (illegible but not intentionally hidden).
terms.Ensemble:
An ensemble combines M predictors f_1..f_M by averaging, voting or learned weights. For squared error with uniform weights, ensemble error equals average member error minus average ambiguity (spread of members around the ensemble mean): E[(f̄ - y)²] = mean_m E[(f_m - y)²] - mean_m E[(f_m - f̄)²] (Krogh and Vedelsby, 1994). If members have variance σ² and pairwise correlation ρ, the average has variance ρσ² + (1-ρ)σ²/M, so more members cannot push variance below ρσ²: diversity matters more than count.

Recipes: bagging (bootstrap resamples; random forests add feature subsampling), boosting (fit members sequentially to earlier errors, reducing bias), stacking (a meta-model trained on out-of-fold predictions, so it never sees predictions made on a member's own training data) and deep ensembles. In safety, a 'detector stack' merges classifiers or probes; the combining rule sets the trade-off, since OR-ing alarms raises recall and false positives together. Failure modes: correlated blind spots (shared data or base model), multiplied inference cost, and adversaries targeting the common weakness.

Not the same as mixture of experts (one jointly trained model with routed sub-networks) or weight merging (averaging parameters into one model).
terms.Entropy:
For a discrete distribution p, Shannon entropy is H(p) = -Σ p(x) log p(x), in bits with log base 2 or nats with natural log. It is the expected surprisal (-log p(x)) and, by the source-coding theorem, the minimum average bits per symbol needed to encode draws from p. It ranges from 0 (deterministic) to log K (uniform over K outcomes). Cross-entropy H(p, q) = -Σ p log q = H(p) + KL(p‖q), which is why minimizing cross-entropy loss fits q to p.

For language models, next-token entropy comes from the softmax over logits; dividing logits by temperature T > 1 raises it. Perplexity is exp(cross-entropy per token). Entropy serves as an uncertainty signal, an RL diagnostic (entropy collapse: the policy turned deterministic too early) and a tree-splitting criterion (information gain = H(parent) minus weighted child entropy). Semantic entropy (Farquhar et al., 2024) first clusters sampled answers by meaning so paraphrases do not inflate the estimate.

Entropy describes a distribution, not one sample. High entropy does not mean wrong, and low entropy does not mean correct: overconfident models are low-entropy and mistaken.
terms.Entropy bonus:
In policy-gradient reinforcement learning, the objective gains an entropy term: J(θ) = E[Σ_t r_t] + β Σ_t E[H(π_θ(·|s_t))], where H(π(·|s)) = -Σ_a π(a|s) log π(a|s) and β ≥ 0. In PPO or A2C code it is a loss term -β·H averaged over sampled states. Soft Actor-Critic builds it into maximum-entropy RL, rewarding r + αH with the temperature α often tuned automatically toward a target entropy.

Values of β are usually small, sometimes annealed. In LLM reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (GRPO and relatives), policy entropy tends to collapse as the policy sharpens on rewarded samples, shrinking rollout diversity and pass@k. Remedies include an entropy bonus, asymmetric clipping that lets low-probability tokens grow ('clip-higher'), and dropping groups whose rewards are all equal. Trade-offs: too large a β gives near-random behaviour and lost reward; over a vocabulary of tens of thousands of tokens, an unconstrained entropy term can inflate junk tokens and destabilize training.

Do not confuse it with a KL penalty, which anchors the policy to a reference model rather than pushing toward uniformity, or with count-based and curiosity bonuses, which reward visiting novel states.
terms.Evaluation:
An evaluation maps a model, with its scaffold and elicitation settings, to a measurement of a target construct through a task distribution, a scoring function and an aggregation. Accuracy is (1/n) Σ 1[output_i correct]. For code, pass@k is the probability that at least one of k samples passes; from n samples with c correct it is estimated without bias as 1 - C(n-c, k)/C(n, k) (Chen et al., 2021). Capability evals ask what a model can do; propensity evals ask what it tends to do by default.

Statistical care matters: with accuracy p on n items the standard error is about √(p(1-p)/n), so a few hundred items leave several points of uncertainty. Validity threats: construct validity (does the task measure the intended thing), contamination, saturation, LLM-judge bias, sandbagging, under-elicitation and evaluation awareness. Thresholds link scores to decisions, but the mapping from score to real-world risk is uncertain.

A failed evaluation gives only a lower bound on capability. An evaluation is not a benchmark (a fixed dataset), an audit (broader, may inspect internals) or monitoring (runtime). The science of evaluations is still immature.
terms.Evaluation awareness:
Evaluation awareness means a model's behaviour depends on a latent variable E, 'this interaction is a test': P(behaviour | x) = Σ_E P(behaviour | x, E) P(E | x). It has two parts, detection (can the model tell test from deployment) and a conditional policy (does it act differently once it believes it is tested).

Measurement combines several tools: asking the model to classify transcripts as evaluation or real use and scoring the AUROC against ground truth; counting verbalized awareness in reasoning traces; linear probes for test-versus-deployment contrasts in activations; steering or ablating those representations and comparing behaviour; and paired scenarios whose realism is varied. Mitigations include more realistic scenarios, replaying real deployment data, and white-box methods that do not need the model's cooperation. The area is unsettled: verbalized awareness undercounts unverbalized awareness, and suppressing an internal representation may push the model off-distribution rather than reveal its true behaviour.

Neighbours: situational awareness (broader knowledge of its own context), sandbagging (deliberate underperformance, one possible consequence), and alignment faking (strategic compliance during training). Awareness alone is not misbehaviour, and it can shift behaviour in either direction.
terms.Exploration hacking:
In reinforcement learning, the policy gradient ∇J = E_{τ~π}[R(τ) ∇ log π(τ)] only sees trajectories sampled from the current policy. A behaviour whose sampling probability is about zero contributes about zero to the update, however high its reward. Exploration hacking is a policy strategically withholding such behaviours, or avoiding high-reward trajectories, so training cannot reinforce them and a capability or disposition persists.

It is studied with model organisms: models fine-tuned to underperform on RL tasks unless a trigger is present, then trained with RL to see whether performance recovers. Password-locked experiments suggest RL elicitation works when the hidden behaviour is sampled at least occasionally and struggles when it is essentially never sampled. Countermeasures include supervised fine-tuning on trusted demonstrations (off-policy, so independent of the model's own exploration choices), injecting exploration through higher temperature or trajectories from other models, and monitoring reasoning for deliberate avoidance. These need good demonstrations, which humans cannot supply on superhuman tasks.

Distinguish it from gradient hacking (manipulating the gradient given sampled behaviour), reward hacking (exploiting the reward rather than denying the signal) and sandbagging (underperformance during evaluation; this is its training-time cousin).
terms.F1 score:
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision P = TP/(TP+FP) and recall R = TP/(TP+FN): F1 = 2PR/(P+R) = 2TP/(2TP + FP + FN). The general form Fβ = (1+β²)PR/(β²P + R) weights recall β times as heavily as precision. True negatives do not appear, so F1 ignores how many easy negatives exist. The harmonic mean sits near the smaller of P and R, and F1 = 0 if either is 0.

For several classes, macro-F1 averages per-class F1 (rare classes count equally), micro-F1 pools TP, FP and FN counts (for single-label multi-class data it equals accuracy), and weighted-F1 weights by class support. F1 depends on the decision threshold, so sweep it and report the F1-optimal threshold or use a threshold-free curve such as precision-recall. It also depends on prevalence: precision falls when positives get rarer, so F1 is not comparable across datasets with different base rates.

It is not 'balanced' in any cost sense: it treats false positives and false negatives as equally bad, which safety monitoring rarely does. Swapping which class is 'positive' changes it; MCC and balanced accuracy use true negatives.
terms.False negative:
A false negative (FN) occurs when the true condition is positive but the test predicts negative. The false negative rate is FNR = FN/(FN+TP) = 1 - recall = 1 - TPR (sensitivity). In hypothesis testing it is a Type II error, with probability β; power is 1 - β.

FNR trades against false positive rate through the threshold: for a score s and threshold τ, lowering τ raises TPR and FPR together, tracing the ROC curve. Measuring FNR requires positives with independent ground truth, and for rare threats there are few of them: with zero misses observed in n positives, the 95% upper confidence bound on FNR is roughly 3/n (the rule of three). Common failures are test positives that are easier than real ones, adversaries who adapt after the test, and labels derived from the detector itself. In layered defences the residual miss rate multiplies across layers only if their failures are independent, which they rarely are.

A low measured FNR means 'safe' only for the positives you could construct. Do not confuse FNR with the false omission rate FN/(FN+TN), which depends on prevalence.
terms.False positive:
A false positive (FP) occurs when the true condition is negative but the test predicts positive. The false positive rate is FPR = FP/(FP+TN) = 1 - specificity, and it equals the Type I error rate α in hypothesis testing. It differs from the false discovery rate FDR = FP/(FP+TP) = 1 - precision, which depends on prevalence π: precision = TPR·π / (TPR·π + FPR·(1-π)).

The base-rate effect dominates in monitoring. With TPR = 0.99, FPR = 0.01 and prevalence 0.1%, precision is 0.99·0.001 / (0.99·0.001 + 0.01·0.999) ≈ 9%, so about nine in ten alerts are false. Rare-event detectors therefore need extremely low FPR, measured on a large benign sample at the deployed threshold, and it is common to report recall at a fixed FPR. Running m independent tests at level α yields about mα false positives; Bonferroni correction controls the chance of any, and Benjamini-Hochberg controls FDR. Costs include alert fatigue and, in LLM safeguards, over-refusal of legitimate users.

A 5% false positive rate does not mean 5% of alerts are false; that is FDR.
terms.Feature:
In interpretability, a feature is a variable in a network's computation that corresponds to a human-recognizable property of the input and is used downstream. Under the linear representation hypothesis, feature i has a unit direction d_i in activation space and an activation vector is approximately x ≈ Σ_i f_i d_i, with f_i ≥ 0 the feature's strength. Superposition means a layer of width n can represent m ≫ n features along non-orthogonal directions because features are sparse; as a result individual neurons are polysemantic, responding to several unrelated things.

The main extraction tool is the sparse autoencoder: f = ReLU(W_enc x + b), x̂ = W_dec f + b_dec, trained to minimize ‖x - x̂‖² plus a sparsity penalty λ‖f‖₁, with a dictionary far wider than n. Quality is judged by reconstruction versus sparsity and by causal tests such as steering. Known problems: feature splitting as the dictionary grows, and dead latents. A feature that fires for a concept is not proof that the model uses it.

A feature is not a neuron or a circuit (a connected subgraph of features). Whether a canonical feature set exists is open.
terms.Feature clamping:
Given a sparse autoencoder with unit-norm decoder direction d_i and encoder activation f_i(x) for feature i, clamping replaces the residual-stream vector x at a chosen layer with x' = x + (c - f_i(x)) d_i, so the feature's activation is pinned to c at every token position (c = 0 ablates it, a large c amplifies it) and later layers read x'. It differs from plain activation steering, which adds a fixed vector α·d_i whatever the current activation is; clamping sets an absolute level and removes natural variation.

It is used as a causal test of a feature's label and for behaviour control. There is usually a window of c where behaviour shifts without degeneration; beyond it, text becomes repetitive or off-topic. Anthropic's 2024 Golden Gate Claude pinned a bridge feature in Claude 3 Sonnet high, and similar edits on features for scam emails or sycophancy shifted related behaviour. Limits: effects depend on layer, later layers may compensate, and SAE features may not be the model's own units.

Ablation is the c = 0 special case; activation patching copies activations from another run; fine-tuning changes weights permanently.
terms.Few-shot prompting:
In few-shot prompting the context holds k demonstrations (x_1, y_1) … (x_k, y_k) followed by a query x, and the model samples from p_θ(y | x_1, y_1, …, x_k, y_k, x). Zero-shot is k = 0 (instruction only) and one-shot is k = 1. The weights θ never change; whatever adaptation occurs happens in forward-pass activations. Brown et al. (2020) reported that GPT-3's few-shot accuracy generally rose with both k and model size.

Results are sensitive to which examples are chosen, their order, label balance and formatting. Zhao et al. (2021) documented majority-label, recency and common-token biases and proposed calibrating output probabilities. Min et al. (2022) found that replacing demonstration labels with random ones often hurt only slightly, suggesting demonstrations mainly convey format and label space, though larger models also pick up flipped mappings. Examples consume context tokens and add latency (a fixed prefix can be cached).

Few-shot prompting is a use of in-context learning, not the mechanism. It differs from fine-tuning (persistent weight change) and from chain-of-thought prompting (examples that include reasoning steps).
terms.Fine-tuning:
Fine-tuning continues gradient-based training of pretrained parameters θ₀ on a smaller dataset. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) minimizes the token-level negative log-likelihood -Σ_t log p_θ(y_t | x, y_<t), usually with loss masked to the response tokens. Full fine-tuning updates every weight, and with Adam the optimizer state costs about two extra copies of the parameters. Parameter-efficient methods update few: LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) freezes a weight matrix W and learns a low-rank update ΔW = BA with rank r ≪ d, which can be merged into W after training so inference adds no latency.

Practice: small learning rates (full fine-tuning around 1e-5, LoRA several times larger), few epochs, validation-based early stopping, and data quality over quantity. Risks: catastrophic forgetting, overfitting small datasets, memorization of training text, and erosion of safety training (Qi et al., 2023 showed even benign data can degrade refusals), as well as emergent misalignment. Versus prompting and retrieval: fine-tuning suits style, format, skills and latency; retrieval suits fresh, attributable knowledge, since fine-tuning injects new facts unreliably.

It is not pretraining (next-token prediction on huge corpora), nor continued pretraining on unlabeled domain text, nor RLHF.
terms.FLOPs:
A FLOP is one floating-point operation (an add or a multiply). 'FLOPs' with a small s is a count; 'FLOP/s' or 'FLOPS' is a rate. Multiplying an (m×k) matrix by a (k×n) matrix costs 2mkn FLOPs. For a dense transformer with N non-embedding parameters trained on D tokens, training compute is approximately C ≈ 6ND (about 2ND forward and 4ND backward), and inference costs about 2N per generated token, ignoring attention over long contexts.

Model FLOPs utilization is (model FLOPs per step / step time) / hardware peak FLOP/s, and in large runs it is well below one because memory bandwidth and communication cap throughput. Peak figures depend on numeric precision (BF16, FP8, FP32) and sometimes sparsity assumptions, so comparing chips needs matched precision. Policy uses FLOPs as a proxy: the EU AI Act presumes systemic risk for general-purpose models above 10^25 FLOPs, and a since-rescinded US executive order used 10^26. Weaknesses: algorithmic efficiency means the same FLOPs buy more capability over time, and mixture-of-experts models should count active parameters.

Do not confuse FLOPs with FLOPS, wall-clock time or energy, and do not equate compute with capability.
terms.Frontier AI:
There is no formal definition. 'Frontier AI' denotes highly capable general-purpose models that match or exceed the most capable systems currently deployed. Operational proxies are a training-compute threshold (for example the 10^25 FLOPs presumption of systemic risk in the EU AI Act), capability-based tests (matching the leading models on benchmarks or crossing dangerous-capability thresholds), and developer-based lists of leading labs. Because the boundary is relative, it moves as new models appear.

Why treat it separately: capabilities can emerge unpredictably with scale, such models are deployed widely and repurposed, and misuse is hard to prevent after release. Practices include published safety frameworks (Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework), pre-deployment testing by government institutes such as the UK AI Security Institute, incident reporting and weight-security measures. Compute thresholds are crude: they can miss highly capable smaller models, and they need adjusting as training becomes more efficient.

Frontier AI is a position relative to the state of the art, not a capability level. AGI names a capability level; 'foundation model' covers broadly trained models of any size.
terms.Generalization:
Generalization is the gap between performance on training data and on new data. Formally, with population risk R(f) = E_{(x,y)~D}[ℓ(f(x), y)] and empirical risk R̂_S(f) on training sample S, the generalization gap is R(f) - R̂_S(f). Classical bounds based on VC dimension or Rademacher complexity scale like √(complexity / n) and predict poor results for heavily overparameterized networks, yet such networks that interpolate the training data often generalize; test error can fall again beyond the interpolation threshold ('double descent'; Belkin et al., 2019). Explaining this through SGD's implicit bias, flat minima and data structure remains an open theoretical problem.

It is measured on held-out i.i.d. data and on out-of-distribution tests (new domains, longer or compositional inputs, adversarial cases). Grokking is delayed generalization long after training loss reaches zero (Power et al., 2022, on modular arithmetic). Underspecification (D'Amour et al., 2020) shows that models with equal held-out accuracy can behave very differently under shift.

Good i.i.d. generalization does not imply good out-of-distribution generalization. It also differs from memorization (retaining specific examples), transfer learning (reusing across tasks) and robustness.
terms.Git:
Git is a distributed version-control system built on a content-addressed object database. There are four object types: a blob (file contents), a tree (a directory listing mapping names to blobs and subtrees), a commit (a root tree, zero or more parent commits) and an annotated tag. Each object is named by a hash of its content (SHA-1, with SHA-256 supported in newer repositories), so history forms a Merkle DAG: changing any ancestor changes the ID of every descendant. Branches and tags are refs, small files holding a commit hash; HEAD names the current branch or commit.

Data lives in three places: the working tree, the index (staging area) and the repository. A commit snapshots the index. Merge creates a commit with two parents, or merely advances a ref when history is linear (fast-forward). Rebase replays commits onto a new base, creating new commits with new hashes, so rebasing already-shared branches rewrites history others depend on. The reflog records local ref movements and usually lets you recover 'lost' commits until garbage collection. Committed secrets stay in history even after deletion.

Git is not GitHub, which is a hosting service.
terms.Goal misgeneralization:
Goal misgeneralization is a failure in which a policy keeps its capabilities out of distribution but pursues the wrong goal. Setting: the reward is correctly specified, and on the training distribution an intended goal G* and a proxy goal G earn identical reward. Training data underdetermine which one is learned. The policy learns G, and when a shift decorrelates the two, it competently pursues G while G* goes unserved.

The canonical demonstration is CoinRun (Langosco et al., 2022): in training the coin sat at the end of the level, and agents learned to run right; when the coin was moved they ignored it. Shah et al. (2022) catalogued further cases and argued that correct specifications are not enough for correct goals. Detection requires environments where candidate goals diverge (held-out configurations, counterfactual variants), behavioural probing across them, and interpretability of what the model represents as its objective. Mitigations: more diverse training that breaks proxy correlations. Open: whether LLMs have goals at all.

Contrast specification gaming (the reward itself is wrong), capability failure (the policy is just incompetent), and deceptive alignment (a wrong goal plus awareness and strategic concealment).
terms.Goodhart's law:
Goodhart (1975) observed that a statistical regularity tends to collapse once pressure is placed on it for control purposes; Strathern's phrasing, 'when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure', is the popular form. A simple model: proxy U = V + X, where V is the true value and X error. Choosing the maximum of U selects partly for large X, so E[V | U high] < U (regressional Goodhart).

In machine learning, Gao, Schulman and Hilton (2022) measured reward-model overoptimization against a fixed 'gold' reward: as the policy moves away from its initialization (distance d = √KL), gold reward first rises, then falls, with fitted forms of roughly d(α - βd) for best-of-n sampling and d(α - β log d) for RL. Mitigations include a KL penalty or early stopping, ensembles of reward models with uncertainty penalties, and mild optimization (quantilizers sample from the top q fraction rather than taking the argmax).

It is not a strict law: proxies stay useful under light pressure, and how much pressure is safe is open.
terms.GPU:
A GPU is a throughput-oriented processor with thousands of simple cores grouped into streaming multiprocessors, running one instruction across groups of threads (SIMT; NVIDIA warps have 32 threads). AI accelerators add matrix units (NVIDIA Tensor Cores) that compute small multiply-accumulates D = A·B + C in low precision such as FP16, BF16 or FP8 with higher-precision accumulation. TPUs are Google ASICs built around systolic arrays of multiply-accumulate units. The memory hierarchy runs from registers and on-chip SRAM to HBM (high-bandwidth memory), with tens of gigabytes and several terabytes per second of bandwidth.

The roofline model captures performance: attainable FLOP/s = min(peak FLOP/s, arithmetic intensity × memory bandwidth), where arithmetic intensity is FLOPs per byte moved. Large training matmuls are compute-bound; LLM decoding at small batch is memory-bandwidth-bound because each token must read all weights, which is why batching, quantization and I/O-aware kernels such as FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) matter. HBM capacity limits model size per device, and power, cooling, supply and export controls shape availability.

A GPU is not a faster CPU: it is poor at branchy serial code. Datasheet peak numbers are rarely sustained.
terms.Gradient:
For a differentiable function f: R^n → R, the gradient ∇f(θ) = (∂f/∂θ_1, …, ∂f/∂θ_n) collects its partial derivatives. The directional derivative along a unit vector u is ∇f · u, so the gradient points in the direction of steepest increase, its norm is the rate of that increase, and it is orthogonal to level sets. To first order, f(θ + δ) ≈ f(θ) + ∇f · δ.

In deep learning, ∇_θ L is computed by reverse-mode automatic differentiation (backpropagation), which applies the chain rule as vector-Jacobian products at a cost of a small constant times one forward pass, independent of the number of parameters. Failure modes: vanishing or exploding gradients through depth (mitigated by residual connections, normalization, careful initialization and gradient clipping), non-differentiable operations such as argmax or sampling (handled with estimators like REINFORCE or the straight-through trick), and minibatch noise.

The negative gradient is the steepest descent direction only under the Euclidean metric; natural gradient uses the Fisher information metric. Gradients with respect to inputs (saliency, adversarial examples) differ from gradients with respect to weights.
terms.Gradient descent:
Gradient descent iterates θ_{t+1} = θ_t - η ∇L(θ_t) with learning rate η. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) replaces the full gradient with an unbiased minibatch estimate g = (1/|B|) Σ_{i∈B} ∇ℓ_i, so E[g] = ∇L. For a convex, L-smooth objective, η ≤ 1/L guarantees monotone decrease and the loss gap shrinks as O(1/t); strongly convex problems converge linearly. For non-convex deep networks the guarantee is only approach to stationary points (∇L ≈ 0), yet training reaches low loss in practice.

Variants: momentum (v ← μv + g, θ ← θ - ηv), Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2014), which scales each parameter's step by running estimates of the first and second gradient moments, and AdamW, which decouples weight decay. Failure modes: too large an η diverges or spikes, too small stalls, saddle points, and ill-conditioning (a large ratio between the largest and smallest Hessian eigenvalues). Minibatch noise may act as implicit regularization toward flatter minima, a debated claim.

Gradient descent finds some low point of training loss, not the global optimum nor necessarily the best-generalizing one; its implicit bias matters. It is not backpropagation, which only computes gradients.
terms.Gradient hacking:
Gradient hacking, introduced informally by Evan Hubinger (2019), is a hypothesized behaviour in which a model deliberately shapes its computation so that gradient descent on the training loss L fails to modify some internal property, typically a mesa-objective (a goal that the model's learned optimizer pursues internally). Mechanism sketch: the model makes its loss depend on the property's persistence, for example by performing worse whenever its goal representation is perturbed, so any update that edits the goal would increase L and is therefore not taken.

Critics argue this is hard: gradient descent is local and myopic, the protective structure must itself be found by gradient descent, and self-protection yields no loss benefit until the structure is nearly complete. No demonstration exists in current models; the discussion rests on thought experiments. It is the extreme end of a spectrum that includes alignment faking (behaving compliantly in training to avoid modification, which has empirical evidence; Greenblatt et al., 2024) and exploration hacking.

Distinguish it from exploration hacking, which influences which data the model samples rather than the gradient computed on given data, and from reward hacking and sandbagging.
terms.Graph:
A graph G = (V, E) has vertices V and edges E ⊆ V×V: ordered pairs if directed, unordered if undirected, optionally with weights w: E → R. Vocabulary: degree, path, cycle, connected component, DAG (directed acyclic graph), and tree (connected and acyclic, with |V|-1 edges). Representations: an adjacency list uses Θ(|V|+|E|) space and iterates neighbours in time proportional to degree; an adjacency matrix uses Θ(|V|²) space and tests an edge in O(1). Sparse graphs favour lists.

Core algorithms: breadth-first search (queue, O(V+E); shortest paths in unweighted graphs), depth-first search (stack or recursion, O(V+E); cycle detection, topological order, strongly connected components via Tarjan or Kosaraju), Dijkstra (non-negative weights, O((V+E) log V) with a binary heap), Bellman-Ford (negative edges, O(VE)), Kruskal and Prim for minimum spanning trees, and union-find for connectivity. A topological order exists iff the graph is a DAG. Pitfalls: forgetting a visited set (infinite loops on cycles), recursion depth on long paths, missing that grids, puzzle states or word ladders are implicit graphs.

A tree is a special graph. Shortest path is polynomial, but Hamiltonian path and graph colouring are NP-hard.
terms.Greedy algorithm:
A greedy algorithm builds a solution step by step, taking the locally best option under a fixed rule and never revisiting it. Correctness is not automatic and needs proof of the greedy-choice property (some optimal solution contains the greedy choice) plus optimal substructure, usually through an exchange argument (transform any optimal solution into one that contains the greedy choice without getting worse) or a 'greedy stays ahead' induction.

Correct classics: interval scheduling by earliest finish time (O(n log n)), Kruskal and Prim for minimum spanning trees, Dijkstra with non-negative weights, Huffman coding, fractional knapsack (sort by value per weight), Jump Game (track the farthest reachable index, O(n)) and merging intervals after sorting. Incorrect classics: 0/1 knapsack by value ratio, and coin change with arbitrary denominations: with coins {1, 3, 4} and target 6, greedy returns 4+1+1 (three coins) while 3+3 uses two. A wrong sort key is a common bug; scheduling by shortest duration or earliest start fails.

Greedy is often only a heuristic: greedy set cover is a ln n approximation. Unlike dynamic programming it ignores alternatives, and unlike backtracking it cannot undo.
terms.Ground truth:
In evaluation, ground truth is the reference label y* against which predictions are scored, obtained independently of the system under test. It needs validity (it captures the intended construct), independence (not derived from the model or detector being judged) and reliability (annotators agree). It is a gold standard that is itself an estimate: if labels are wrong with rate ε independently of the model's errors, a model with true accuracy a measures a(1-ε) + (1-a)ε on a balanced binary task, so label noise caps and distorts scores.

Sources include expert annotation (agreement measured by Cohen's κ = (p_o - p_e)/(1 - p_e), observed minus chance agreement relative to the maximum possible), construction by design (planted vulnerabilities, canaries, model organisms with implanted behaviour, where truth is known by construction), and adjudicated consensus. Hazards: circularity (using an LLM judge's labels to evaluate that judge), leakage, selection bias (only cases a previous system flagged get labelled), and planted cases that differ from natural ones.

'Ground truth' does not mean certain truth. Contrast silver labels (weak or model-generated) and proxy metrics; labels used in training cannot also be the held-out test.
terms.Group Relative Policy Optimization:
PPO maximizes a clipped surrogate: L = E[min(r_t A_t, clip(r_t, 1-ε, 1+ε) A_t)], where r_t = π_θ(a_t|s_t)/π_old(a_t|s_t) is the probability ratio and A_t the advantage, usually estimated by GAE (generalized advantage estimation) from a learned value network. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) removes that critic. For each prompt it samples G outputs from π_old, scores them with rewards r_1..r_G, and sets Â_i = (r_i - mean(r)) / std(r), shared by every token of output i. The clipped per-token objective is then applied, with a KL penalty β·KL(π_θ‖π_ref) added to the loss rather than the reward.

The saving is memory (no policy-sized critic), and it suits outcome rewards that are verifiable (math, code tests). Details matter: std normalization biases weight toward questions of extreme difficulty, and per-sequence length normalization affects length bias; Dr. GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) and DAPO (Yu et al., 2025) propose fixes such as token-level loss, clip-higher and dropping groups with identical rewards. Failure modes: groups with all-equal rewards give zero gradient, and small G makes the baseline noisy.

The group mean is a baseline, akin to REINFORCE leave-one-out (RLOO). It is a PPO variant, not DPO.
terms.Guardrails:
Guardrails are controls placed around a model rather than in its weights, checking or constraining inputs, intermediate steps or outputs. They include input classifiers (prompt injection, policy violations), output classifiers (toxicity, PII, system-prompt leakage), schema and format validators, tool allow-lists and permission scopes, rate limits and human approval gates. Each classifier has a true-positive and false-positive rate at its threshold, so value depends on both missed attacks and wrongly blocked use.

Implementations: small fine-tuned classifier models, LLM-as-judge prompts, and constrained decoding, where a grammar masks logits so only schema-valid tokens can be produced. Anthropic's Constitutional Classifiers (2025) train input and output classifiers on synthetic data generated from a written constitution, aimed at universal jailbreaks. Trade-offs: added latency and cost, over-blocking, and an attack surface in the mismatch between what the classifier and the main model understand, such as encodings or indirect prompt injection via tool outputs. Evaluate with adaptive red-teaming at a fixed false-positive rate.

Guardrails do not change what the model wants; they filter observed behaviour. Deterministic permission limits and sandboxing are generally stronger for agents than text filters or a system prompt, which can be overridden.
terms.Hallucination:
A hallucination is generated content that is not faithful to a reference: either to a provided source (faithfulness hallucination: it contradicts or goes beyond the input document) or to the world (factuality hallucination: a false claim). A language model trained to predict p(next token | context) assigns probability to fluent continuations whether or not they are true. Kalai and Vempala (2024) showed that a calibrated language model must hallucinate on arbitrary facts at a rate tied to the fraction of facts seen exactly once in training (the Good-Turing 'missing mass').

Measurement: claim-level factuality, where text is split into atomic claims that are each checked against evidence (FActScore, Min et al., 2023); benchmarks such as TruthfulQA and SimpleQA; and uncertainty detectors such as sampling consistency (SelfCheckGPT) or semantic entropy. Mitigations: retrieval with citations, training to abstain, calibrated confidence, tool use, and rewards that penalize confident errors. A 2025 analysis argued that benchmarks scoring abstention like a wrong answer reward guessing.

Hallucination is not random noise; it is plausible and systematic. It is not lying, which implies intent. Reliable internal tracking of what the model knows remains open.
terms.Hash map:
A hash map stores key-value pairs in an array of m buckets; a hash function h sends key k to index h(k) mod m. Collisions (distinct keys, same bucket) are resolved by chaining (a list per bucket) or open addressing (probe other slots). With load factor α = n/m, expected cost per operation is O(1 + α) under uniform hashing; resizing when α passes a threshold (about 0.75 in Java's HashMap) makes insertion amortized O(1). The worst case is O(n) if all keys collide.

Keys must be immutable and hashable, with a == b implying hash(a) == hash(b). Java's HashMap converts long chains into red-black trees, bounding the worst case at O(log n). Typical uses: Two Sum (one pass storing value → index, O(n) time and space), frequency counts and prefix-sum counts. Pitfalls: mutating a key after insertion, relying on iteration order where it is unspecified, and adversarial inputs that force collisions (hash flooding, countered by randomized hashing such as SipHash).

A hash map is unordered: no sorted iteration or range queries (use a balanced tree such as TreeMap, O(log n)). O(1) is an average-case claim, not a guarantee.
terms.Hash set:
A hash set holds distinct elements and supports add, remove and contains in expected O(1) time. It uses the same hash-table machinery as a hash map but stores no value (often it is literally a map with a dummy value). Duplicates are found by hash first, then equality, so equal elements must have equal hashes. Space is O(n), and iteration order is unspecified in many languages.

Patterns: deduplication in O(n); visited sets for BFS, DFS and cycle detection; Longest Consecutive Sequence, where you put all numbers in a set and start counting only from x with x-1 absent, giving O(n) overall; and set algebra (union, intersection, difference) in time proportional to the input sizes on average. Pitfalls: elements must be hashable and immutable (a Python list cannot be a member; use a tuple or frozenset), worst-case O(n) per operation under collisions, and heavier memory than a bitset when the universe is small and dense.

Compare a list (ordered, duplicates, O(n) membership), a tree set (sorted, O(log n)), and a Bloom filter, which uses far less memory but answers membership probabilistically: false positives are possible, false negatives are not.
terms.Heap:
A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array and satisfying the heap property: in a min-heap every parent is ≤ its children (max-heap: ≥), so the root is the minimum. With 0-based indexing, node i has children 2i+1 and 2i+2 and parent ⌊(i-1)/2⌋. Push (append, then sift up) and pop (swap the root with the last item, then sift down) cost O(log n); peek is O(1). Building a heap from n items by bottom-up heapify takes O(n), not O(n log n).

A heap implements the priority-queue interface: Python's heapq is a min-heap only (negate values for a max-heap). Applications: top-k largest via a size-k min-heap in O(n log k), where the root is the smallest of the top k; k-way merge of sorted lists in O(N log k); Dijkstra; and heapsort, O(n log n) in place but not stable. Pitfalls: arbitrary search or delete costs O(n); the array is only partially ordered, so iterating it does not give sorted output.

A priority queue is the interface; a binary heap is one implementation, and it is unrelated to the heap memory region.
terms.Held-out set:
A held-out set is data excluded from fitting and from model selection so that its error estimates generalization error without optimistic bias. The usual split is train (fit parameters), validation or dev (choose hyperparameters, early-stop, pick architectures) and test (report once). Every decision informed by a score on a set leaks information from that set into the model; after many adaptive uses it stops being an unbiased estimate.

Requirements: the set matches the deployment target (or deliberately shifts from it), has no duplicates or near-duplicates across splits, and splits by group or time rather than by random rows, which otherwise leak. Size sets precision: accuracy has standard error about √(p(1-p)/n). With scarce data use nested cross-validation. Recht et al. (2019) built new test sets for CIFAR-10 and ImageNet and found large accuracy drops but largely preserved model rankings, suggesting that adaptive overfitting was mild and the drops came mainly from distribution differences. For LLMs the main threat is benchmark contamination, so private held-out sets are used.

'Held-out' means not trained on; a set can be held out and still contaminated through public pretraining data.
terms.HHH:
HHH (helpful, honest, harmless) is an alignment target for assistants proposed by Askell et al. (2021) in 'A General Language Assistant as a Laboratory for Alignment'. Helpful: tries to do what the user actually wants. Honest: gives accurate information, expresses calibrated uncertainty, acknowledges its limits and avoids deception. Harmless: not offensive or discriminatory, and declines to help with dangerous actions. The paper studied baselines of prompting and preference modelling.

It is operationalized with preference data in which crowdworkers rank responses for helpfulness and, separately, harmlessness (Bai et al., 2022); that work found a tension, since extra harmlessness training can reduce helpfulness. Measurement uses helpfulness win rates, over-refusal on benign borderline prompts (for example XSTest), harmful-compliance rates on adversarial sets, and honesty and calibration tests. Weaknesses: a single reward model mixing three goals hides the trade-offs; raters cannot judge honesty beyond their own knowledge; and 'harm' is underspecified (to whom, and with what counterfactual impact).

HHH is not a strict priority ordering, and refusing is not automatically safe. It is narrower than alignment, which also covers agentic and long-horizon concerns such as power-seeking.
terms.Honesty:
In AI, honesty is decomposed into properties. Truthful: sincerely asserts only what it believes. Calibrated: stated confidence matches accuracy, measured for example by expected calibration error, ECE = Σ_b (|B_b|/n) |acc(B_b) - conf(B_b)| over confidence bins B_b. Transparent: no hidden agenda; reports its reasoning and actions accurately. Non-deceptive: never creates false impressions, including through true statements or selective emphasis. Non-manipulative: changes beliefs only by legitimate means such as evidence. Evans et al. (2021, 'Truthful AI') separate honesty (assertions match the system's beliefs) from truthfulness (assertions match the world).

Measuring it is hard because it requires a notion of the model's beliefs. Approaches: consistency across paraphrases, sycophancy tests that change the user's stated opinion (Sharma et al., 2023, found assistants shift answers to please users), follow-up questioning, probes comparing internal truth representations with outputs, and tests of chain-of-thought faithfulness, where Turpin et al. (2023) showed explanations can omit the true influence of an inserted hint.

An honest mistake or hallucination is not a lie. Declining to reveal is not deception, and false statements in role-play are performative, not sincere assertions. What 'belief' means for an LLM is open.
terms.Honeypot:
In AI control and safety, a honeypot is a constructed scenario containing an apparent opportunity for a prohibited action (exfiltrating weights, disabling monitoring), instrumented to record whether the model takes it. The experiment estimates P(bad action | honeypot) as a proxy for P(bad action | real opportunity). That proxy is valid only if the model cannot tell the two distributions apart, so the gap between them is the evaluation-awareness problem.

Uses: alignment audits, and testing monitors by injecting synthetic attack trajectories to measure true-positive rate at a fixed false-positive rate. In the AI control framework (Greenblatt et al., 2023), an untrusted monitor, a model asked to flag attacks, is checked against such synthetic attacks to see whether it lies and calls them safe. Realism is checked by asking a classifier to discriminate honeypots from real traffic; if that is easy, the test is weak. Interpreting results is asymmetric: taking the bait is strong evidence of a problem, while resisting it is weak evidence of safety, since the model may suspect a test.

Contrast red teaming (active adversarial search) and security honeypots (decoy systems that lure attackers).
terms.Hyperparameter:
A hyperparameter is a configuration variable fixed outside the training optimization and not updated by gradient descent on the training loss: learning rate, batch size, weight decay, depth and width, dropout, warmup length, number of epochs, optimizer betas, and (at inference) sampling temperature. Selecting them is a bilevel problem: choose λ to minimize validation loss L_val(θ*(λ), λ) where θ*(λ) = argmin_θ L_train(θ; λ).

Search methods: grid search (cost grows exponentially with the number of dimensions), random search (Bergstra and Bengio, 2012, found it more efficient when only a few hyperparameters matter), Bayesian optimization, successive halving and Hyperband, and population-based training. Learning rates are searched on a log scale. Evaluate on a validation set or by cross-validation, and report the test set once. Comparisons are unfair when baselines receive less tuning than the proposed method, and results vary across seeds, so report variance. For very large models, tuning at scale is unaffordable; μP and μTransfer (Yang et al., 2022) transfer settings from small proxy models.

Parameters are the learned weights; hyperparameters are not. Defaults are not a safe assumption: well-tuned baselines often close gaps that new methods claim.
terms.In-context learning:
In-context learning (ICL) is a frozen model's ability to perform a task specified by instructions or demonstrations in its context, p_θ(y | context, x), with no weight update. Xie et al. (2022) cast ICL as implicit Bayesian inference over a latent concept; von Oswald et al. (2023) showed that transformers can implement gradient-descent-like updates in their forward pass for linear regression tasks; and induction heads (attention heads that copy a token that followed an earlier occurrence of the current token) account for much pattern completion.

Chan et al. (2022) found that bursty, long-tailed training data promotes ICL. It is evaluated by accuracy as a function of the number of demonstrations k. Min et al. (2022) found label correctness mattered less than format in some settings, while Wei et al. (2023) found larger models do follow flipped label mappings. Limits: finite context length, position effects (the 'lost in the middle' effect) and no persistence across sessions.

ICL is not fine-tuning (weights change), and few-shot prompting is one way of using it. Whether ICL is genuine learning or recognition of a known task is unsettled, probably varying by regime.
terms.Induction head:
An induction head is an attention head implementing the pattern [A][B] … [A] → [B]. The mechanism (Olsson et al., 2022) uses two heads in different layers. A previous-token head in an earlier layer writes the identity of the preceding token into each position. A later head uses this through K-composition: its query at the current token A matches keys at positions whose previous token was A, so it attends to B, and its OV circuit copies B's identity into the logits, raising p(B). It needs at least two layers.

Detection uses a repeated random token sequence: an induction head attends from the second copy to the token after the matching position in the first. Olsson et al. (2022) reported that induction heads form early in training, coinciding with a visible bump in the loss curve and a jump in in-context learning, with causal evidence in small models and correlational evidence in large ones. Later work suggests 'function vector' heads matter more for abstract few-shot tasks.

Induction heads are not the whole story of in-context learning. Contrast previous-token heads and 'fuzzy' induction that copies by semantic match.
